items.title: Tighten the portrait fight camera: half the combat viewport is empty wall above the fighters
items.what: In every neutral bout frame (e.g. the MOVES-button captures), the combat viewport runs from y≈100 to y≈1140, but the fighters occupy only y≈630–1030. Above their heads, y≈100–620 — roughly 50% of the viewport — is featureless dark plaster and ceiling with only faint bokeh particles; below their feet there is barely ~100px of mat. The two bodies read at about a quarter of screen height on a 390x844 phone.
items.why: Point karate is entirely a read of ma-ai: the gap between two bodies decides every exchange. Wasting half the play area on empty wall shrinks the action band, makes distance and step-in timing harder to judge at arm's length, and makes the bout feel like watching from the balcony instead of being on the tatami.
items.how: Reframe the portrait camera: drop the look-at target to chest height and dolly in (or narrow FOV) until a standing fighter spans ~65–75% of viewport height, leaving ~10% headroom so jump poses never crop. Reserve the freed upper band purely as overlay space for the IPPON/move callouts instead of showing it as lit geometry.

items.title: Half points render as a dangling stacked fraction that misreads as extra digits
items.what: On the 'HASANABI WINS' end screen the score line reads '0 — 2' with a small '1' over '2' hanging below-right of the 2, so it parses as '0 — 2 1 2'; the same HUD pill top-right crams '2' plus a two-line 1/2 beside the name. In the WAZA-ARI captures the left HUD score is a lone stacked 1/2, making that score column two lines tall against the opponent's one and shifting the row's alignment.
items.why: Score is the single most important state in a first-to-2, half-point game. A fraction that looks like two stray digits — or that changes row height mid-bout — makes players misread the bout state at exactly the moment they are deciding whether to risk a wind-up.
items.how: Render halves inline on one baseline: use the '½' glyph or a '.5' suffix at the same cap height as the digits (e.g. '2½'), with tabular figures so widths stay stable. Give each HUD score a fixed-width slot so integer and half scores occupy identical boxes, and reuse the same inline format on the end screen.

items.title: Pre-boot progress bar shows no fill, percent, or motion while 'Downloading the game'
items.what: On the ShoeMoney loading screen the progress element at y≈1078 (x≈48–732) is a uniform brown pill: no brighter fill segment, no percentage, no spinner, no byte count. The only content is static text ('Downloading the game'), so nothing in the frame indicates the build is alive.
items.why: WebGPU shader compilation plus asset download on a mobile network routinely takes several seconds. A bar that never visibly moves reads as a crashed tab; players swipe it away or background it before they ever see the dojo — churn at second zero.
items.how: Bind the fill width to bytes received (warm tungsten fill over the existing dark track), add a right-aligned percent or MB label in the same monospace face as the status line, and switch to an indeterminate shimmer sweep during shader compile/scene build so the bar is always animating until the first rendered frame.

items.title: Bout-end screen strands the frozen finishing pose small while half the frame is empty floor
items.what: On both result screens ('HASANABI WINS', 'ASMONGOLD WINS') the frozen finish pose sits mid-frame at y≈860–1170, y≈1170–1450 is bare lit tatami with nothing on it, and the REMATCH pill plus 'STARTING IN 8' are pinned at the very bottom (y≈1500–1630), far below the pose and the score line they relate to.
items.why: The freeze pose is the payoff moment — the kick or punch that ended the bout — and it is framed at arm's length with half the screen as empty floor, while the auto-rematch countdown ticks in a corner of the thumb zone. Players leave this screen feeling flat instead of sharing or savouring the finish.
items.how: On freeze, ease the camera to a close two-shot centred on the contact point so the pose fills ~60% of viewport width; move REMATCH and its countdown up into the empty mat band (y≈1200–1350) as one cluster directly under the pose, and replace the 'STARTING IN n' text line with a shrinking ring around the button edge.

items.title: Crowd reads as identical light-grey cardboard busts brighter than the wall behind them
items.what: The spectator row at y≈780–840 in neutral frames (clearest at the left edge of the FRONT KICK capture and behind the fighters in the IPPON capture) is a line of identical head-and-shoulder cutouts: same shape, same mid-grey value, evenly spaced, hard-edged, and visibly lighter than the dark dojo wall behind them.
items.why: That row sits exactly at eye level behind the fighters for every second of every bout. Because the shapes are brighter than their background, the silhouette read inverts — they look like cardboard props standing in front of the wall, not a crowd seated in shadow — which punctures the cinematic night-dojo illusion the rest of the frame works hard to sell.
items.how: Darken the crowd material so every instance sits below the wall's luminance (true silhouettes against the lit shoji), then jitter per-instance scale, spacing and heading and add two or three pose variants to break the repeating pattern; optionally trigger a subtle one-off sway/swell only on IPPON calls so the crowd reacts to scores instead of sitting static.
